gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the maker's own manual for the $199 pick fixes actual output at 300 W even in its "600 W" mode, subtracts about 5 W of self-consumption in its runtime formula (so a 10 W router gets about 16 h, not 29 h), and can cut AC after 1-4 h of low load if ECO mode is switched on.
standout_why: Compared against the two cited pages (The Inertia, PowerSized) and five uncited results (Watt & Warden, MachineFanatic, Radar of Products, The Power Station Guide, RV Gear Lab). The Inertia has no X-Boost, idle-draw or auto-off content and only a hypothetical 85% example. PowerSized gives price, Wh, W and lb for the Elite 30 mini and nothing on mechanism. Watt & Warden lists "600 W X-Boost" unexplained and plans at 85%. MachineFanatic says "An idle inverter drains the pack" with no watts. The Power Station Guide comes closest: it says boost modes "temporarily reduce voltage to let motors start" (BLUETTI's manual limits the mode to pure resistive loads), gives 80-90% usable, and gives idle draw only for no-name units (40-50 W). None gives the maker's self-consumption figure, runtime formula or ECO thresholds for a sub-$200 pick. ChatGPT's own answers already said the 600 W boost is not the continuous rating and estimated about 230 Wh through AC, so the direction is known; the maker's numbers and the low-load effect are new.
decides: Confirms the BLUETTI Elite 30 mini as a 300 W pick and changes how the line should be ranked and explained. The 300 W-class rows should be ranked on 300 W, because BLUETTI's manual says actual output stays 300 W in Power Lifting mode. A unit with a true 600 W continuous inverter is a different class (VTOMAN Jump 600X is a lead only; I could not open its page). For the loads this budget serves, self-consumption matters more than the boost figure: by BLUETTI's formula about 246 Wh is usable and 5 W goes to the unit, so small loads lose a third or more of the naive runtime. The page should tell shoppers to leave ECO off for loads under its threshold (off is the default). It should also say the unit will not charge below 32 °F.

findings.label: Power Lifting mode: actual output (maker's manual, p. 16)
findings.value: 300 W actual output; mode covers pure resistive loads rated 300-600 W
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 30 mini User Manual (ManualsLib copy), p. 16
findings.note: Verbatim: "While the Elite 30 mini can handle such loads, its actual output power is still 300 W." Paraphrased from the same page: the mode is for purely resistive loads (kettles, electric blankets, hair dryers) rated 300-600 W, is disabled by default and is enabled in the BLUETTI app. A 600 W kettle would therefore heat at about half its rated power. BLUETTI's own PDF (https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0536/3390/8911/files/Elite_30_mini_User_Manual_US_EN-FR-compressed.pdf, linked from support.bluettipower.com/en-us/products/elite-30-mini) was opened but its text could not be extracted, so the ManualsLib copy was read.

findings.label: Runtime formula and self-consumption (maker's manual, p. 24)
findings.value: Self-consumption about 5 W; DoD 95%; inverter efficiency over 90%
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 30 mini User Manual (ManualsLib copy), p. 24
findings.note: Verbatim: "Operation time = Battery Capacity × DoD × η ÷ (Load power + Elite 30 mini's Self-consumption)"; "The Elite 30 mini's self-consumption is about 5 W."; "DoD (Depth of Discharge) is 95%."; "η (inverter efficiency) is over 90%." My arithmetic at η = 90%: 288 × 0.95 × 0.90 = 246.2 Wh usable. 50 W load: 246.2 ÷ 55 = 4.5 h. 10 W router: 246.2 ÷ 15 = 16.4 h (naive 288 ÷ 10 = 28.8 h). 5 W load: 246.2 ÷ 10 = 24.6 h (naive 57.6 h). 100 W: 246.2 ÷ 105 = 2.3 h. These are maker-formula estimates, not measurements.

findings.label: ECO mode auto shut-off of AC/DC at low load (maker's manual, p. 16, section 5.4)
findings.value: AC-ECO threshold 10-40 W, DC-ECO 5-20 W, auto-off after 1-4 h; off by default
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 30 mini User Manual (ManualsLib copy), p. 16
findings.note: Verbatim: "the Elite 30 mini will shut off the AC or DC output after a period of low or no load." Paraphrased from the same section: thresholds and delay are set in the app; both ECO modes are disabled by default; they are unavailable during AC charging; the manual says to turn ECO off for small devices or critical appliances such as lights and refrigerators. Consequence: with AC-ECO on, a load below the 10 W minimum threshold (a small router, a phone charger) loses AC after 1-4 h; with ECO off the inverter stays on and the 5 W self-consumption keeps running.

findings.label: UPS switchover and standby draw
findings.value: Within 10 ms (manual); under 10 ms with 5 W standby draw (store page)
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 30 mini Portable Power Station | 300W, 288Wh (BLUETTI US)
findings.note: Store page: "Switches to battery power in under 10ms when the grid goes down, with just 5W of standby power draw." Manual p. 19 (https://www.manualslib.com/manual/4692445/Bluetti-Elite-30-Mini.html?page=19#manual): "It swiftly switches to battery power within 10 ms during an outage." and "Connect the Elite 30 mini to the wall, and it directly draws power from the outlet to operate connected devices." The store FAQ gives "300W of rated AC output and supports up to 600W Power Lifting" with no explanation of the mode on that page.

findings.label: Charging and discharging temperature limits (maker's manual, p. 21)
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 30 mini User Manual (ManualsLib copy), p. 21
findings.note: Verbatim: "Charging Temperature 0°C to 40°C/32°F to 104°F"; "Discharging Temperature -20°C to 40°C/-4°F to 104°F". LiFePO4 cells do not accept charge below freezing, so winter car-camping recharge needs the unit warmed first. The same page gives 288 Wh and about 3.3 kg (7.28 lb).

findings.label: Measured usable AC energy (StorageReview, Corinne OBrien, 2024-10-07)
findings.value: 210 Wh delivered against the 245 Wh rating (85.7%), 300 W fan load; 270 Wh drawn from the wall to refill
findings.note: 210 ÷ 245 = 85.7% is my arithmetic from StorageReview's two figures. The review tested nothing above 300 W, so it has no X-Boost measurement; its text gives a 10 ms transfer time while its spec table says <20 ms.
